A1.justification: Both PDFs describe WT-ASBS and contain readable main text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices. Retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original peptide and reaction sampling experiments, including free-energy estimates, convergence comparisons, computational timings, and distributional metrics.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original hyperparameter and training ablations plus a learned-CV experiment on alanine dipeptide.

M1.justification: v2 adds an implemented variant using a separately trained Deep-TDA network to supply a one-dimensional collective variable (F.4), whereas v1 only suggested learned CVs. The WT-ASBS update rules, losses, replay-buffer algorithm, and main sampler architecture remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate alanine dipeptide, alanine tetrapeptide, nucleophilic substitution, and post-transition-state bifurcation. The new ablations and learned-CV experiment retain the alanine-dipeptide equilibrium-sampling task; they change configurations and procedures rather than molecular or task coverage.

E2.justification: Corresponding comparisons retain WTMetaD, ASBS, and MD, while Table 2 retains PIS, DDS, AS, NAAS, and ASBS. The added experiments introduce ablated configurations and reference-distribution comparisons, not additional external baseline methods.

E3.justification: v2 substantially expands evaluation design with controlled bias-parameter sweeps, AM-update and pretraining comparisons, and a learned-CV setup using 5,000 configurations per state. Table 1 changes dipeptide h from 1e-4 to 5e-4 eV, SN2 stages from 4 to 2, and bifurcation stages from 2 to 4. D.4 changes the bifurcation WTMetaD bias factor from 20 to 30. These reported revisions do not establish that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New Appendix E systematically tests Gaussian height, width, bias factor, AM updates between buffer refreshes, and pretraining, tracking both convergence and intermediate sampling distributions. F.4 adds a learned-CV case study examining recovered free energies and residual distortion along an insufficiently resolved coordinate.

E5.justification: The four-repeat WTMetaD descriptions and Table 2 uncertainty reporting are retained. The additions do not introduce new seed counts, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty-estimation procedures.

E6.justification: Figures 7–13 add substantial convergence and sampling results: excessive Gaussian height impairs final convergence, too few AM updates slow adaptation, and pretraining accelerates convergence. Figure 18 adds learned-CV free-energy agreement alongside broadened psi-direction modes. Original Table 2 scores, benchmark plots, and reaction timing figures are retained; these additions do not demonstrate improved performance in the original settings.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions, objectives, Proposition 3.1, and its Appendix B proof are retained. The new discussion of imperfect-sampler reweighting qualifies practical applicability without changing the formal results or derivations.

C1.justification: The abstract and principal introduction contributions remain unchanged. The discussion now includes demonstrated compatibility with learned CVs as an achieved capability, extending what v1 presented primarily as a prospective application.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly limits exact bias reweighting to a perfectly trained sampler and discusses refinement and path-weight alternatives. It explains why tetrapeptide free-energy error does not beat WTMetaD, connects buffer-refresh failures to inadequate sampler adaptation, and qualifies learned-CV performance through known-state requirements and poor psi resolution. These substantially expand the practical interpretation and limitations.

D1.justification: v2 replaces Code: TBA with a repository link, adds convergence-based guidance for selecting training duration, and documents the learned-CV inputs, 24/12-unit hidden layers, target distributions, and training data. Existing implementation documentation is largely retained, with several reported hyperparameters revised.

R1.justification: New A.3 substantially broadens positioning relative to learned transition-path sampling and data-trained thermodynamic generators, discussing works by Holdijk, Du, Seong, Wang, Herron, Qiu, and Benayad and Stirnemann. It distinguishes equilibrium configuration sampling from trajectory generation and data-based approaches; the discussion also adds connections beyond molecular sampling.

P1.justification: The main narrative and methods structure remain largely intact. v2 rewrites the discussion, expands selected explanations, inserts an extended related-work subsection and an ablation appendix, and moves the former Additional Results appendix from E to F.

P2.justification: v2 adds extensive convergence plots and bias/sample grids in Figures 7–13, plus the learned-CV panels in Figure 18. Original supplementary Figures 7–10 become Figures 14–17. Main figure captions are expanded and retained figures and tables are repositioned.

improvement.justification: v1 left the practical bias-update and replay-buffer choices largely unsupported by sensitivity analysis. v2 directly tests these choices, identifies failure regimes, and explains their relationship to the idealized algorithm, substantially strengthening methodological validation. The learned-CV demonstration and more candid exactness and accuracy qualifications further improve the paper. The gains remain bounded: new analyses concentrate on alanine dipeptide, add no uncertainty procedures, and do not establish improved original benchmark performance.
